title: Parity-Resolved Quantum Capacitance and Quantum Inductance in Topological, Trivial, and Normal Nanowire Interferometers
authors: Viktoriia Pinchenkova, Valerii K. Kozin, Maximilian Hünenberger, Daniel Loss, Jelena Klinovaja
abstract: Quantum-capacitance measurements convert the curvature of a quantum-dot energy in a flux-threaded nanowire loop into fast parity-sensitive signals and, therefore, have become a promising readout tool for Majorana devices. However, Majorana-like quantum-capacitance responses can also arise from topologically trivial Andreev bound states, making capacitance alone insufficient to identify a topological phase. To analyze this problem, we consider a quantum dot coupled to both ends of four nanowire realizations: a topological nanowire hosting Majorana bound states, non-topological superconducting nanowires hosting one or two Andreev bound states, and a fully normal nanowire. Motivated by proposals to use quantum inductance as an additional phase-sensitive probe, we compute both the parity-resolved quantum capacitance $C_\mathrm{Q}$ and inverse quantum inductance $L_\mathrm{Q}^{-1}$ as functions of the magnetic flux by exact diagonalization. We show that signatures associated with zero-energy Majorana bound states, such as $h/e$ periodicity and an $h/(2e)$ flux shift between even and odd parity sectors in $C_\mathrm{Q}$ and $L_\mathrm{Q}^{-1}$, are not sufficient indicators of topological superconductivity. In certain realistic parameter regimes, similar Majorana-like behavior can arise from a trivial Andreev bound state and even from a purely normal nanowire. By contrast, two nearly zero-energy Andreev bound states can generate a pronounced $h/(2 e)$-periodic component associated with charge-$2e$ transfer, providing a clear non-Majorana signature. A low-energy projection shows that the Majorana, single-Andreev-state, and normal cases can be mapped onto the same minimal low-energy model explaining their similar flux-dependent responses despite their different physical origins.
summary: The paper investigates whether quantum capacitance and inductance measurements can uniquely identify Majorana bound states in nanowire interferometers. By comparing results from topological, trivial, and normal wire models, the authors demonstrate that similar flux-dependent signatures are not exclusive to MBSs. They propose that more complex diagnostics, such as observing specific charge-$2e$ periodic components, are necessary for definitive topological identification.
main_problem: To determine if characteristic quantum capacitance ($C_Q$) and inverse quantum inductance ($L_Q^{-1}$) oscillations are uniquely indicative of topological Majorana bound states (MBSs), or if similar signatures can arise from trivial superconducting physics.
main_result: The standard Majorana-like patterns observed in $C_Q$ and $L_Q^{-1}$ are not unique to the topological phase, as they can emerge from trivial Andreev bound states or normal wires. A clear non-Majorana signature was found using two nearly zero-energy ABSs.
method: The authors computed parity-resolved quantum capacitance and inverse quantum inductance by exactly diagonalizing the system Hamiltonian for four different nanowire realizations (topological, single/two-ABS, normal).
model_or_system: The study analyzes a quantum dot coupled to an interferometer loop formed by various superconducting or normal nanowires. The model uses a 1D Rashba nanowire Hamiltonian and calculates observables using the Bogoliubov–de Gennes framework.
key_observables: Parity-resolved quantum capacitance ($C_Q$) and inverse quantum inductance ($L_Q^{-1}$), measured as functions of magnetic flux ($\Phi$).
important_parameters: Magnetic flux ($\Phi$), superconducting gap ($\Delta$), coupling amplitudes ($\lambda_L, \lambda_R$), and disorder strength ($\delta\mu$).
main_assumptions: The analysis compares results from topological, single-ABS, two-ABS, and normal wire regimes; the effective model relies on perturbative expansion for small couplings.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the four different nanowire setups (Topological, Trivial, Non-topological, Normal) and show calculated $C_Q(\phi)$ and $L_Q^{-1}(\phi)$ curves for various regimes.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the problem of distinguishing topological signatures from trivial ones using capacitance/inductance. It details the theoretical framework by calculating observables in the full model, deriving an effective low-energy Hamiltonian, and comparing results across different physical realizations (topological vs. non-topological).
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major experimental challenge in condensed matter physics: developing unambiguous signatures to confirm topological superconductivity using transport measurements.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Different interferometric setups considered in this work. A Rashba nanowire (NW) is aligned along the x axis. The SOI vector points in the z direction and the magnetic field in the x direction. A quantum dot (gray) is coupled to the left and right ends of the NW, forming an interferometric loop that encloses a magnetic flux Φ. (a) The NW is covered by a superconductor, which induces superconductivity (S) via the proximity effect. The NW is tuned to the topological regime, where it can host MBSs localized at its ends. (b) The NW is tuned to the trivial phase. The left segment is not covered by the superconductor and remains normal (N), allowing for an ABS localized near the S–N...

FIG. 2. (a) Energy spectrum of the nanowire uncoupled from the QD in the topological interferometer, as a function of the Zeeman energy ∆Z. (b) Probability density of the MBSs and the lowest-energy bulk state at ∆Z = 0.675 meV [indicated by the black line in (a)]. The chosen ∆Z lies in the topological phase and yields nearly zero MBS energy splitting, resulting in states localized at the nanowire ends with negligible over- lap. The parameters are listed in Table I in Appendix E.

FIG. 3. (a) Low-energy spectrum of the topological interfer- ometer. (b) Difference between quantum capacitance in the even and odd parity sectors ∆CQ as a function of VQD. (c), (e) Even and odd branches of the quantum capacitance CQ and (d), (f) the quantum inductance L−1 Q at VQD = 0.75 meV and VQD = 0.82 meV [indicated by the black lines in (b)]. In all presented cases, CQ(ϕ) and L−1 Q (ϕ) exhibit a 2π-periodicity and π phase shift. The effective model [dashed lines in (c)- (f)] reproduces the results of the full Hamiltonian (solid lines). The parameters are listed in Table I in Appendix E.

FIG. 4. (a) Energy spectrum of the nanowire uncoupled from the QD in the non-topological interferometer with one ABS. (b) Probability density of the ABS at the Zeeman energy ∆Z = 1.26 meV [indicated by the black line in (a)]. The chosen ∆Z, together with a small superconducting gap ∆0 = 0.09 meV, results in a finite probability density at the right end of the nanowire, allowing the ABS to couple to the QD from both ends. The parameters are listed in Table II in Appendix E.

FIG. 5. (a) Low-energy spectrum of the non-topological in- terferometer with one ABS. (b) Difference between quantum capacitance in the even and odd parity sectors ∆CQ as a function of VQD. (c), (e), (g) Even and odd branches of the quantum capacitance CQ and (d), (f), (h) quantum in- ductance L−1 Q at VQD = 1.425 meV, VQD = 1.38 meV and VQD = 1.48 meV [indicated by the black lines in (b)]. In this parameter regime, CQ(ϕ) and L−1 Q (ϕ) show Majorana-like be- havior, namely 2π periodicity and nearly π phase shift. The parameters are listed in Table II in Appendix E.
